Chapter 4: Generosity, Self-Denial, and the True Measure of Faith
Let’s be honest—most of us grow up in a world that tells us the goal is to have more. More savings, more stuff, more security. Giving? Sure, that’s encouraged—but only after we’ve made sure all our own needs and wants are covered.
But when you look at the life of Jesus and his earliest followers, you see something completely different. For them, generosity wasn’t an occasional act. It was a way of life.
Picture this: a group of friends hears about a family down the street who’s hit a rough patch. They decide to pool their money to help. Suddenly, they’re skipping dinners out, putting off that weekend getaway, maybe even selling a few things they don’t really need. At first, it stings. There’s that nagging worry—what if there’s not enough left for us?
But something unexpected happens. The joy they get from helping outweighs the sacrifice. They start to realize that real wealth isn’t about what you keep—it’s about what you give away.
Now, if that sounds difficult, you’re not alone. Most of us are taught to see what we own as a measure of success or a safety net. Shifting away from that mindset? It’s tough. It means trusting there’ll be enough, even when giving feels risky.
But Jesus didn’t just talk about giving money. He called his followers to something even deeper—to deny themselves, take up their cross, and follow him.
That’s not just about finances. It’s really about letting go of the need to always be in control, to always be comfortable, to have life play out exactly how we want. It’s about putting other people’s needs before our own, and trusting that God is going to provide—no matter what.
There’s a story I love about a single parent who barely made ends meet. Even though money was tight, this person made a habit of inviting neighbors over for dinner whenever they saw a need. Sometimes, there just wasn’t enough to go around. But as the weeks went by, something changed. The act of giving—of sharing what little they had—became a source of strength and joy. The friendships that grew out of those meals? They were worth more than anything money could buy.
Here’s something to think about: most of us don’t realize how much we’re driven by our need for comfort and security. But the challenge of generosity and self-denial is an invitation to let go of that. It’s a reminder that faith isn’t measured by what we keep for ourselves—it’s measured by what we’re willing to give away.
So, take a look at your own life. Where is there a chance to give a little more, to serve a little more, to set aside comfort for the sake of someone else? This kind of journey isn’t easy—but it’s the path to a deeper, more authentic faith.
